In 26.0.0-BETA.2, Docker can't pull nontrivial images in *privileged* container
column5:
See my and other folks' debugging on [this forum thread|https://forums.truenas.com/t/truenas-26-beta-1-lxc-docker-real-images-fail-with-failed-to-register-layer-operation-not-permitted-dev-fuse-unavailable/65762] for all the backstory. Keeping it short here:

* Create a new LXC in TrueNAS with ID Map Type = Privileged and Capabilities Policy = Allow All.
* Install Docker in the LXC.
* Inside the LXC, update {{/etc/docker/daemon.json}} to enable IPv6 (else Docker errors out for reasons I think are unrelated to this bug) and restart Docker.
* Inside the LXC, pull an image with nontrivial layers, e.g., {{docker pull lscr.io/linuxserver/radarr:latest}}.

Notice that the pull fails. See forum thread for the various errors you can get, and some messing about with trying to switch to the {{fuse-overlayfs}} driver, which shouldn’t be needed, and fails regardless (even if {{/dev/fuse}} is manually passed through to the container).

Instead, what _does_ seem to fix the issue is [manually editing in an idmap that is basically 1:1 for all users|https://forums.truenas.com/t/truenas-26-beta-1-lxc-docker-real-images-fail-with-failed-to-register-layer-operation-not-permitted-dev-fuse-unavailable/65762/16?u=bcat]: 

{noformat}  <idmap>
    <uid start='0' target='0' count='2147483648'/>
    <gid start='0' target='0' count='2147483648'/>
  </idmap>{noformat}

TrueNAS UI won’t let you do that, but if you {{virsh edit}} it in manually, Docker seems to pull and start images just fine inside the container, and it appears that users / groups in the container are still correctly mapped 1:1 in host filesystem mounts.

I guess Docker _needs_ a nested {{userns}} for some reason. I have no idea why, nor why this doesn’t seem to be a problem for the other (more common?) LXC impls that other OSes use.

I am a little hesitant to suggest that TrueNAS’s “privileged containers” should always add such an {{idmap}}, as I don’t understand _why_ it works, but if there are no side effects, it might be a reasonable workaround. (And I suspect running Docker in LXCs is a pretty common use case, as it enables full control over networking, etc. while still allowing Docker containers to share TrueNAS filesystem mounts.)

column4: VDEV description cosmetic bug
High CPU usage due to CLI redraw if a key input is stuck
column5:
Community Reported, original URL and text body below.

A stuck physical key or emulated virtual key through IPMI/OOB means can trigger this behavior.

The {{/usr/bin/cli --menu --pager}} process will lock a thread to 100%, causing increased CPU power consumption, thermal output, and reduce potential peak performance.

Source: [https://www.reddit.com/r/truenas/comments/1ue00w4/comment/oti04nq/|https://www.reddit.com/r/truenas/comments/1ue00w4/comment/oti04nq/] 

*You can peg your CPU Thread at 100% with a keyboard!*

{quote}Something interesting for everyone.

So my server is running on an 8/16 modern Intel CPU, which I noticed suddenly doubled in temperature. Still safe, but certainly not a measurement error.

I'm running the latest non-beta SCALE.

I noticed this issue...:

CPU pegged at 100% by /usr/bin/python3 /usr/bin/cli --menu --pager on tty1

System appeared idle but one process (cli --menu --pager) was constantly using 100% CPU and 3ish GB RAM.

This fellas Process was tied to [+getty@tty1.service+|mailto:getty@tty1.service] (local console).

Reboot/restart of getty didn’t fix it initially because the process immediately respawned (expected, but I was looking for a software loop).

Turns out, a pen was left on the keyboard tray when slid back, and the physical server keyboard had its spacebar held down.

This was generating a continuous stream of input events into the TTY session - Seems like the TrueNAS CLI was taking each keypress and continuously redrawing the interface.

I'm guessing the CLI --menu --pager interface likely performs a full redraw every input event? (since it's just expecting 1~10)

Stuck key means high event rate means tight event loop: input>redraw>input>redraw = load! Took a while to hunt this down actually.

No obvious kernel errors or hardware faults, process _looked_ like a daemon issue (clearly wasn't), restarting services didn’t help because the keyboard remained stuck.

Seems like we need to throttle this UI loop?

Whats even stranger to me, when I turned the monitor on to look, the repeat rate wasn't actually very high maybe 5 a second - Perhaps this was throttled by the fact the thread was pegged at 100%, but it shouldn't be that heavy of a task.{quote}

column4: Replication fixes
UPSLoadPlugin mislabels Netdata Watts chart as Percentage (regression from nut_ups.load → load_usage)
column5:
1. Steps to reproduce:
- Configure NUT (local or remote/slave mode) with a UPS exposing ups.load and ups.realpower.nominal but no direct ups.power/ups.realpower reading (e.g. CyberPower BR650ELCD via usbhid-ups).
- Confirm real load via `upsc <ups>@<host>` (e.g. ups.load: 30, ups.realpower.nominal: 390).
- Open Reporting > UPS > "UPS Input Load."
- Query Netdata directly to confirm chart units:
  curl -s "http://localhost:6999/api/v1/chart?chart=upsd_local_<identifier>.load_usage" | grep units
  -> returns "units":"Watts"
- Confirm a separate, correct percentage chart already exists:
  curl -s "http://localhost:6999/api/v1/charts" | grep -B5 '"context":"upsd.ups_load"'
  -> upsd_local_<identifier>.load_percentage, units: "percentage"

2. Expected Result:
"UPS Input Load" should show load as a percentage (e.g. ~30%), matching `ups.load` from `upsc`.

3. Actual Result:
"UPS Input Load" shows ~113-117 (Watts, calculated as load% x realpower.nominal), mislabeled with a Percentage axis. Root cause: UPSLoadPlugin in src/middlewared/middlewared/plugins/reporting/netdata/graphs.py points get_chart_name() at Netdata's `upsd_<id>.load_usage` chart (units: Watts) instead of the correctly-labeled `upsd_<id>.load_percentage` chart (units: percentage). This is a regression — 3 years ago the same class pointed at `nut_ups.load`, a genuine percentage chart, before the Netdata reporting migration changed the chart name without updating vertical_label.

Fix (tested locally, confirmed working):
Change line ~478 of graphs.py from:
    return f'upsd_{self.UPS_IDENTIFIER}.load_usage'
to:
    return f'upsd_{self.UPS_IDENTIFIER}.load_percentage'
Restarting middlewared after this change produces correct output (confirmed matching upsc: Max 30, Mean 29.1, Min 28).

Enhancement suggestion: since Netdata exposes both load_percentage and load_usage as separate charts for the same UPS, consider adding both as separate reports (e.g. "UPS Input Load %" and "UPS Input Power (Watts)") rather than only fixing the mislabeling, since absolute Watts draw is useful for capacity planning alongside relative %.

I discovered this while using the Proxmox plugin. My TrueNAS NVMe-TCP subsystem is configured with associated hosts so only my servers can access it. Seemingly whenever TrueNAS adds a new namespace to the subsystem (and in some interval, at least daily it seems) TrueNAS will reinitialize the nvme kernel system.

{noformat}nvmet: Can't set allow_any_host when explicit hosts are set!{noformat}

Existing namespaces will still work but any new namespace will not be accessible. 

The service can be made to work again by a) allowing all hosts always or b) removing all hosts and then readding them. Both followed by a restart (b another restart in between).

The TrueNAS WebUI also _seems_ to catch this error since the “Allow all hosts” button is missing whenever it occurs despite hosts still being listed. I need to manually remove all hosts. When readding them the button appears again as normal.

column4: mail.send omits Cc recipients from the SMTP envelope, so Cc addresses never receive the email
column5:
{{mail.send}} adds Cc addresses only as a {{Cc:}} header, but the SMTP envelope ({{RCPT TO}}) is built from the To recipients alone. SMTP delivery is driven by the envelope, not the headers, so Cc recipients never receive the message when sending through an SMTP server.

On master ({{src/middlewared/middlewared/plugins/mail/send.py}}):

{code:python}msg["To"] = ", ".join(to)
if message.get("cc"):
    msg["Cc"] = ", ".join(message["cc"])
...
server.sendmail(
    msg["From"],
    msg["To"].split(", "),   # only To -- Cc is never in RCPT TO
    msg.as_string(),
){code}

Scope:

* SMTP path only. The Gmail OAuth path ({{mail.gmail_send}}) submits the raw message to the Gmail API, which parses To/Cc from the headers and delivers to both, so Cc works there. The inconsistency between the two paths is itself a smell.
* Present on both master and stable/26 (in the pre-refactor {{src/middlewared/middlewared/plugins/mail.py}}: {{server.sendmail(from_addr, to, msg.as_string())}}, where {{to}} is the To list only). Long-standing -- the recent master refactor ([NAS-141132|https://ixsystems.atlassian.net/browse/NAS-141132]) preserved the behavior verbatim, so this is not a regression.
* No {{bcc}} field exists in the mail API model, so only Cc is affected.
* No internal caller passes {{cc}} (alerts, cron, and failover all send to To only); impact is limited to external/UI/script callers using an SMTP (non-Gmail) server.

Fix: include the Cc addresses in the recipient list passed to {{server.sendmail}} (and mirror the fix in the stable/26 code path).

Found while reviewing [#19345|https://github.com/truenas/middleware/pull/19345].

Existing App keeps invalid NVIDIA GPU UUID after GPU replacement (TrueNAS SCALE 25.10.4)
column5:
Hello,

I believe I found a bug related to NVIDIA GPU assignment in TrueNAS SCALE 25.10.4.

Background

My system was originally using an NVIDIA RTX 3080.

I later replaced it with an NVIDIA RTX 3060 Ti.

The NVIDIA driver was reinstalled correctly, and the new GPU is detected without any issues.

The following commands report the correct GPU UUID:

nvidia-smi -L
midclt call app.gpu_choices

Both report:

GPU-899dd4a1-ac45-57c5-019a-08b06c7172d3
Problem

An existing Plex application (plex2) worked before the GPU replacement.

After replacing the GPU, enabling GPU acceleration from the Apps UI causes the container to fail during startup with:

failed to create shim task:
failed to get device handle from UUID:
Not Found

Inspecting the application configuration shows that it still contains a different GPU UUID:

"resources": {
  "gpus": {
    "nvidia_gpu_selection": {
      "0000:02:00.0": {
        "use_gpu": true,
        "uuid": "GPU-00ef4f92-c70a-446a-8248-d61c7fac9f07"
      }
    }
  }
}

That UUID does not exist anymore.

Docker receives this stale UUID through DeviceRequests and NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, causing container creation to fail.

Additional observations
Docker GPU support works correctly.
docker run --gpus all ... nvidia-smi works correctly.
The middleware correctly detects the current GPU and its UUID.
Creating a new Plex application (plex3) and assigning the same GPU works perfectly.

This suggests that existing application configurations may retain an obsolete GPU UUID after a GPU replacement, and editing the application from the UI does not refresh it with the current UUID.

Expected behavior

When an existing application is edited and an NVIDIA GPU is selected, the stored GPU UUID should be updated to match the current UUID reported by app.gpu_choices.

I hope this information helps identify the issue.

Thank you.

column5:
h2. Background

The middleware {{container.*}} API has moved on since the WebUI last synced against it (early May 2026). Below are the behavioural changes we made on the middleware side that the UI needs to adapt to. How the UI adapts — where a progress dialog goes, where an extra checkbox lives — is entirely up to the WebUI team.

Unless a point says otherwise, every change below is in *both master (27.0) and stable/26 (26.0.0-RC.1)*, so the UI needs to handle it for the 26.0 release, not just for 27.

h2. 1. {{container.delete}} is now a job

{{container.delete}} is a long-running job (per-container-id lock). It stops the container when asked to, tears down the libvirt domain, and destroys the container's ZFS dataset before it returns — so it can take a meaningful amount of time.

Because the UI negotiates {{legacy_jobs: false}} on connect, calling it as a plain method still returns the real result and still surfaces the real error, so nothing is silently broken today. What is lost is everything the job gives you: progress, job logs, the ability to leave the dialog, and the entry in the Jobs list.

{quote}*stable/26:* applies there too.{quote}

h2. 2. {{container.delete}} takes a second {{options}} argument

Signature is now {{container.delete(id, options)}}. {{options}} is optional and both members default to {{false}}:

* {{force}} — the container is stopped first if it is not already stopped. Without it, deleting a running or suspended container is now refused up front; previously it just went ahead and tore the container down.
* {{recursive}} — the container's dataset is destroyed together with its child datasets and snapshots, any clones of those snapshots wherever in the pool they live, and any holds on them. Releasing a hold can break a replication task that depends on it. Nothing destroyed this way is recoverable. Without it, deleting a container whose dataset has children or snapshots is refused.

Both refusals happen before anything is touched, so the container is left exactly as it was.

The {{recursive}} case is the one that actually needs UI work. Container datasets are not excluded from periodic snapshot tasks, so a pool-root recursive snapshot task is enough to make a container permanently undeletable from the UI, since there is currently no way to send the option. The {{force}} case has an obvious workaround (stop, then delete), but it is worth offering directly.

{quote}*stable/26:* applies there too, with the same option names and the same two refusals.{quote}

h2. 3. {{status.state}} can be {{SUSPENDED}}

{{ContainerEntry.status.state}} is one of {{RUNNING}}, {{STOPPED}}, {{SUSPENDED}}. It was {{RUNNING}} / {{STOPPED}} before.

Anywhere the UI treats "not RUNNING" as "stopped" is now wrong. Middleware treats anything other than {{STOPPED}} as active: renaming a suspended container is refused (that guard previously applied only to {{RUNNING}}), deleting one without {{force}} is refused, and its device operations are refused.

Sizing note: middleware exposes no suspend/resume endpoint, so a container only reaches {{SUSPENDED}} out of band — a libvirt I/O-error pause, or {{virsh suspend}}. It is a real state the API can return and the UI should not fall over on it, but it is not a common path.

{quote}*stable/26:* applies there too.{quote}

h2. 4. NIC MAC addresses are colon-separated only

Custom MACs on NIC devices are now validated as colon-separated only. Dash-separated ({{10-66-6A-1F-F1-B1}}), no-separator, mixed-separator and Cisco dotted ({{1066.6a1f.f1b1}}) forms are rejected; they were accepted before. libvirt only ever parsed the colon form, so the permissive values saved fine and then failed at container start — hence the tightening. Existing rows were normalized by a migration.

This applies to *both container and VM NIC devices*, so the VM device form needs the same treatment.

{quote}*stable/26:* applies there too.{quote}

column4: Make target unregistration safe against queued sysfs works
column5:
None PR: https://github.com/truenas/scst/pull/116

Writing a target's "enabled" sysfs attribute queues a work item and waits for it at most 15 seconds. On timeout the write returns -EAGAIN but the work stays queued and executes whenever a sysfs thread gets to it, potentially long after scst_unregister_target() has started for that target. Removing the sysfs attributes there only stops new writes, not already queued works. The work's kobject reference keeps the scst_tgt memory alive while the driver side is torn down underneath it, and the target leaves its template's tgt_list only after release() returns, so a queued work had nothing to check either.

On a production FC system this executed a stale enable_target() work about 24 seconds into target teardown while the target driver module was unloading. The re-armed, half torn down port then took an ELS in hard IRQ context with ha->tgt.tgt_ops already cleared and panicked (see the earlier qla2x00t-32gbit commits that NULL check ha->tgt.tgt_ops in IRQ reachable paths and fail target enable when qlt_lport_register() fails for the driver side hardening).

Close the window in the core, following the existing tgtt_active_sysfs_works_count pattern of
scst_unregister_target_template()

* A new tgt_unregistering flag and tgt_active_sysfs_works_count are added to struct scst_tgt, both protected by scst_mutex. scst_unregister_target() sets the flag and drains the count before removing the sysfs attributes and calling release().
* New helpers scst_check_grab_tgt_ptr() and scst_ungrab_tgt_ptr(), matching the existing tgtt and devt helper pairs, gate every queued work that can call into the target driver. That covers the enable/disable work and also the rel_tgt_id work, which calls is_target_enabled().
* The cpu_mask work bails out on the flag before calling report_aen(). It runs entirely under scst_mutex, so the flag check alone is race free there.
* __scst_is_relative_target_port_id_unique() skips targets that have started unregistering, since they stay on tgt_list after release() has freed the driver's per target data and must not receive is_target_enabled() calls.
* The failure path of scst_register_target() applies the same guard. It previously freed the target, embedded kobject included, while works could still be queued holding kobject references. It now sets the flag, drains the count and waits for all kobject references to be dropped before the free.
* The three copies of the unlock, msleep, relock drain loop (template, target, device handler) become one helper, scst_wait_no_sysfs_works(), which warns every 10 seconds about what it is still waiting for instead of hanging silently when a driver callback gets stuck.
* A legitimate disable racing unregistration now returns success instead of -ENOENT, since teardown disables the target anyway. A stale enable is still refused.
* The old qla2x00t driver called scst_unregister_target() with tgt_host_action_mutex held, while its enable_target() callback takes the same mutex, which the new drain would turn into an ABBA deadlock. REMOVE_TARGET now drops the mutex across the unregistration and q2t_target_release() acquires it itself for the teardown. The sBUG_ON in q2t_add_target() becomes a graceful -EEXIST, since a racing add can now legitimately see the old target still present.

The drain waits only for works already executing a driver callback. Still queued works keep the count at zero and become no-ops when they run, so a caller executing on a sysfs work thread (a del_target management work for example) cannot deadlock against a queued enable work. No scst_unregister_target() caller holds scst_mutex.

column4: isert-scst fix NULL deref in isert_pdu_err on connection teardown
column5:
None PR: https://github.com/truenas/scst/pull/120

A buggy initiator rapidly connecting and disconnecting over iSER can panic the target. isert_send_data_rsp posts SCSI data and status responses directly, bypassing iscsi_get_send_cmnd, so a posted response never gets write_processing_started set. When the connection is torn down mid I/O, req_cmnd_release_force therefore treats the posted response as never sent and drops its only reference, the same reference the send completion handler drops again once the flushed WR error CQE is reaped. The first put recycles the PDU back into the tx pool, which memsets the embedded iscsi_cmnd, and the stale completion then dereferences the zeroed conn pointer in isert_pdu_err.

{code:language=none}

BUG kernel NULL pointer dereference, address 0000000000000008 Workqueue isert_cq_000000008e39f804 isert_cq_comp_work_cb [isert_scst] RIP isert_pdu_err+0xd/0x40 [isert_scst]
Call Trace
 isert_poll_cq+0x1f6/0x390 [isert_scst]
 isert_cq_comp_work_cb+0x1d/0x50 [isert_scst]
 process_one_work+0x194/0x350
 worker_thread+0x1a1/0x310
 kthread+0xfc/0x240
 ret_from_fork+0x22e/0x260
 ret_from_fork_asm+0x1a/0x30
{code}

Fix the ownership at the root. Mark responses posted by isert_send_data_rsp with write_processing_started under write_list_lock so teardown leaves wire owned responses to their completion handler, and release the wire references at the failure site when posting fails since no completion will ever arrive. Add the same failure handling to isert_process_all_writes. As defense in depth, keep recycled tx pool PDUs pointing at their connection, matching the rx recycle path, and bail out of isert_pdu_err when conn is NULL.

column4: App upgrade job reports SUCCESS when the image pull fails (custom apps)
column5:
Clicking Update on a custom app whose "docker compose pull" fails produces a job
that finishes in about a second with state SUCCESS and progress "App successfully
upgraded and redeployed". Nothing was pulled and nothing was redeployed. The only
visible symptom is the update badge coming straight back a moment later.

The failure is real and it is logged, but only to /var/log/app_lifecycle.log. It
never reaches the UI or core.get_jobs.

CAUSE

src/middlewared/middlewared/plugins/apps/upgrade.py, in upgrade_impl() on master
(the same block is in AppService.upgrade() on 25.10.6):

    try:
        pull_images_internal(context, app_name, app, AppPullImages(redeploy=True), ...)
    finally:
        app = context.call_sync2(context.s.app.get_instance, app_name)
        if app.upgrade_available is False or app.custom_app:
            context.middleware.send_event('app.query', 'CHANGED', id=app_name, fields=app.model_dump())
            job.set_progress(100, 'App successfully upgraded and redeployed')
            return app

A return inside finally discards whatever exception is in flight. For a custom app
the "or app.custom_app" term makes that branch unconditional, so the CallError
raised by compose_action() is always swallowed and the job gets marked SUCCESS.

Refreshing the app state there is reasonable and worth keeping. It's only the
return that's the problem.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE WRONG STATUS

Both steps that follow the pull in pull_images_internal() get skipped when it
raises:

  - the clear_update_flag_for_tag loop, so the update flag stays set
  - app.redeploy, so nothing is recreated

The app is left untouched, the alert stays, and the job claims it worked. Retrying
just repeats it.

STEPS TO REPRODUCE

1. Create a custom app with two services: one referencing a locally built image
   tag that doesn't exist in any registry, one a normal registry image.
2. Wait until the registry image has an update so the Update button lights up.
3. Click Update.

Result: the job goes SUCCESS in about a second, the badge reappears, and the error
is in app_lifecycle.log only.

Real example from my system. "authentik" is a custom app with a locally built
authentik-plexfix image alongside stock postgres and redis:

    [2026/08/02 19:47:10] (ERROR) app_lifecycle.compose_action():58 - Failed 'pull'
    action for 'authentik' app:  worker Skipped - Image is already being pulled by
    server \n postgres Pulling \n server Pulling \n redis Pulling \n postgres Pulled
    \n server Error pull access denied for authentik-plexfix, repository does not
    exist or may require 'docker login': denied: requested access to the resource is
    denied\n redis  Interrupted\nError response from daemon: pull access denied for
    authentik-plexfix, repository does not exist or may require 'docker login':
    denied: requested access to the resource is denied\n

Three upgrade attempts that day all recorded SUCCESS.

Worth noting "redis  Interrupted" in that output. compose_action() runs
"docker compose pull --policy always" across the whole project, so one unpullable
image aborts the pulls for the other services. That's what makes this easy to hit
on any custom app mixing a local build with registry images, and pull_policy: never
or adding a build: section don't help because --policy always overrides both. I'm
not asking for that behaviour to change here, just explaining how the pull ends up
failing.

EXPECTED

The job fails with the CallError from compose_action() so the error surfaces in
the UI.

SCOPE

Only app.upgrade runs the pull action. app.update and app.redeploy call
compose up --force-recreate without pull_images=True, so they aren't affected.
Catalog apps take the non-custom path and aren't affected either.

FIX

PR against master: https://github.com/truenas/middleware/pull/19506

column4: Drop kernel address refresh re-announcements in netlink monitor
column5:
27.0.0-BETA.1 PR: https://github.com/truenas/middleware/pull/19510

The kernel re-emits RTM_NEWADDR every time a router advertisement refreshes an address lifetime. Each refresh became an ipaddress.change event that restarted ix-vendor.service, every few seconds behind routers with aggressive RA timers.

IFA_CACHEINFO carries creation and update timestamps that are equal only for a brand new address, so refreshes are dropped at parse time with no state tracking needed. Messages without cacheinfo pass through and RTM_DELADDR is never filtered.

Restarts now allow a single waiter on the lock instead of silently skipping, so the latest address state is always applied without piling up. Verified against a live kernel on real hardware.

This was pointed out in https://ixsystems.atlassian.net/browse/NAS-141358 and a fix was proposed in https://github.com/truenas/middleware/pull/19401. This fix supersedes that one.

column4: sunrpc: treat empty auth.unix.gid replies as negative entries
column5:
27.0.0-BETA.1 PR: https://github.com/truenas/linux/pull/337

An *AD*/*winbind* customer reported intermittent per-user "*permission denied*" on NFS shares ([SEE-597|https://ixsystemsinc.atlassian.net/browse/SEE-597]). On a server running {{rpc.mountd --manage-gids}}, standard for AD and LDAP environments, a brief winbind or sssd outage makes mountd answer the group lookup with zero groups, and the kernel caches that as a valid answer: the uid loses all supplementary groups on every export for up to mountd's TTL (30 minutes by default), long after the directory service recovers. Only supplementary-group access breaks, so it presents as a random denial that fixes itself. The bug is 19 years old, present since the {{auth.unix.gid}} cache was added in v2.6.21 (2007) and triggerable since mountd started sending zero-group failure replies in 2008, so every kernel we ship is affected.

Applied upstream to the [nfsd-testing branch|https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/cel/linux.git/log/?h=nfsd-testing] of the NFSD maintainer tree (cel/linux) as commit [e865ae5|https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/cel/linux.git/commit/?h=nfsd-testing&id=e865ae50d85a5585eb29cd67dfb0f776da1aa0c9]. It carries Fixes: and Cc: stable, so it will be backported to the affected stable series (including v6.12 and v6.18) automatically once it reaches mainline.

Upstream commit message, as applied:
{code:language=none}

sunrpc: treat empty auth.unix.gid replies as negative entries
When rpc.mountd cannot resolve a uid (getpwuid() or getgrouplist()
failure, e.g. while winbind or sssd is briefly unreachable), it
answers the auth.unix.gid upcall with zero groups. unix_gid_parse()
installs that as a valid positive entry, and svcauth_unix_set_client()
then replaces the credential's group list with the empty one on
every request, RPCSEC_GSS included via svcauth_gss_set_client().
One failed lookup strips that uid of all supplementary groups on
every export for up to mountd's configured TTL (30 minutes by
default), long after the NSS backend has recovered.

mountd cannot send an empty list for a successful lookup, since
getgrouplist(3) always includes at least the user's primary group,
so a zero-group reply can only mean the lookup failed. Record it as
a negative entry: unix_gid_find() then returns -ENOENT and
svcauth_unix_set_client() keeps the groups the RPC credential
already carries. This is the fallback that
commit 3fc605a2aa38 ("[PATCH] knfsd: allow the server to provide a
gid list when using AUTH_UNIX authentication") promised when no
answer is available, and the same state try_to_negate_entry()
already creates when no listener holds the channel open.

Fixes: [3fc605a2aa38](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/cel/linux.git/commit/?id=3fc605a2aa38) ("[PATCH] knfsd: allow the server to provide a gid list when using AUTH_UNIX authentication")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org

Signed-off-by: Ameer Hamza <ameer.hamza@truenas.com>
Link: https://patch.msgid.link/20260814221953.108837-2-ameer.hamza@truenas.com
Signed-off-by: Chuck Lever <cel@kernel.org>

column4: scst keep the old acg installed during session reassignment
column5:
None PR: https://github.com/truenas/scst/pull/123

scst_check_reassign_sess() cleared sess->acg for the whole time it rebuilt the session's tgt_dev list. That window includes one synchronize_rcu() call per replaced or deleted LUN and the session stays fully visible to its initiator throughout. Activity suspension does not close the window. scst_post_rx_mgmt_cmd() queues a newly received task management command to the active list unconditionally, the TM thread picks it up immediately, and the first statement of scst_mgmt_cmd_init() dereferences mcmd->sess->acg before the scst_get_mcmd() suspension check runs. An ABORT_TASK arriving while its own session was mid reassignment therefore crashed the TM thread with a NULL pointer dereference at offset 0x464, which is acg_black_hole_type. Every task management function is affected because the dereference precedes the switch on the function code.

Fix this by leaving the old acg pointer installed until the existing single assignment of the new acg near the end of the function. The session holds a reference on the old acg until scst_put_acg() runs and scst_mutex is held across the whole window, so the pointer stays valid. An audit found no code that depends on sess->acg being NULL during reassignment. The one helper that runs inside the window, scst_alloc_add_tgt_dev(), has used acg_dev->acg instead since upstream commit e7179af46 fixed the same class of crash in 2014. Lockless readers now see the coherent old group instead of NULL, which is already how acg_black_hole_type changes are observed. This also covers the same latent dereferences in iscsi-scst session creation and in the copy manager. Upstream SCST still has this bug and it is reported there as issue 367.

column4: scst do not hold a list cursor across the scst_acg_del_lun mutex drop
column5:
None PR: https://github.com/truenas/scst/pull/126

scst_unregister_device() and scst_unregister_virtual_device() walked dev->dev_acg_dev_list with list_for_each_entry_safe() while calling scst_acg_del_lun() on each entry. That function is not atomic under scst_mutex. After unlinking the acg_dev it drops the mutex to wait for outstanding commands and for an RCU grace period, then relocks and frees. Any acg_dev teardown that wins the mutex during that window invalidates the walker's saved next pointer. Target unregistration is such a teardown. scst_del_acg() unlinks each acg_dev from the device side only, leaving it on acg->acg_dev_list with its device side list entry poisoned, and defers the free to the acg release work. When the device walker resumed on that stale cursor it looked the entry up again by LUN, found the half deleted node, and performed a second list_del() on the poisoned entry. With list hardening that is a general protection fault on LIST_POISON2. Without it the same race can write through reused slab memory, free the acg_dev twice, and underflow the device refcount.

Fix this by restarting from the list head on every iteration instead of carrying a cursor across the call. Both functions now share a new scst_dev_del_all_luns() helper so the loop and its locking assumption live in one place. The list is read again under
scst_mutex after scst_acg_del_lun() returns, so entries removed by a concurrent teardown are simply no longer seen. Progress is guaranteed because an entry present on dev->dev_acg_dev_list is always still findable in its group while scst_mutex is held, so each call removes the first entry.

This was hit in production on an HA system during failover. The scst service restart was tearing down all iSCSI targets while iscsid was logging out the initiator sessions to the peer node, whose pass through devices carry LUNs in both the dying target's group and the copy manager group. The same window exists upstream and the crash is unfixed there. The sanitized oops and the log leading up to it follow. Device, target, and dataset names were replaced and everything else is verbatim.

column4: Set unicast_src_ip for VRRP instances so IPv6 adverts are received
column5:
27.0.0-BETA.1 PR: https://github.com/truenas/middleware/pull/19527

keepalived binds the unicast receive socket to the advert source address. Without unicast_src_ip it uses the first address it learns on the interface, which for IPv6 is the link-local address. The peer sends adverts to our configured address, so they are never delivered and both controllers become MASTER for every IPv6 VIP. IPv4 only worked because the first learned address is normally the configured one. Set unicast_src_ip to the address the peer is configured to send to for every instance.

column4: Identify USB passthrough devices by their physical port in the VM and Container UI
column5:
h2. Background

A USB passthrough device can be identified either by the physical port it is plugged into or by its vendor and product ID. Both are supported and neither is going away. The port is the better default: it survives replugs and reboots, and it can tell two identical devices apart, which vendor/product cannot.

Middleware exposes the device list through {{vm.device.usb_passthrough_choices}} and {{container.device.usb_choices}}. Both return the same thing — one entry per connected device, keyed by port, carrying that device's vendor ID, product ID and a human-readable description.

Today the VM UI records the port. The container UI reads the same list but discards the port and records vendor/product instead, which is why two identical devices cannot both be attached to a container.

h2. What we want

Both the VM and container UIs should allow a device to be selected by port or by vendor/product, defaulting to the port.

* Containers should record the port when a device is picked from the list, the same as VMs already do.
* Vendor/product stays available on both. Devices already recorded that way must keep displaying and remain editable — upgraded systems carry them.
* Choices should be presented using the human-readable description middleware returns rather than the raw identifier, and entries middleware flags as unusable should be skipped.
* Containers should allow USB devices to be attached at creation time and edited afterwards; neither is possible today.

h2. Scope

Needed on both {{master}} and {{stable/26}}.

column4: nfsd: don't modify a session slot when replaying its cached reply
column5:
27.0.0-BETA.1 PR: https://github.com/truenas/linux/pull/344

An NFS customer hit repeated kernel panics on their file servers ([SEE-604|https://ixsystemsinc.atlassian.net/browse/SEE-604]), three faults across two 6.12.91 appliances. An NFSv4.1 client that loses its connection retransmits, and if the connection drops again before the reply arrives, two copies of the same request reach the server at once. Both are answered from the session reply cache, which should be read-only, but since v5.10 a cached reply also rewrites the slot it just read from with no lock held. One thread frees and rebuilds the cached credential while another compares against it, and nfsd takes a NULL dereference and panics. Only a connection dropping twice is needed. The bug has been there since [cc028a10a48c|https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/cel/linux.git/commit/?id=cc028a10a48c] in v5.10-rc1 (2020), so both truenas/linux-6.12 and truenas/linux-6.18 are affected.

The fix was [posted to linux-nfs|https://lore.kernel.org/linux-nfs/20260824173641.3274260-1-ameer.hamza@truenas.com/] and applied upstream to the [nfsd-testing branch|https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/cel/linux.git/log/?h=nfsd-testing] of the NFSD maintainer tree (cel/linux) as commit [e74f668|https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/cel/linux.git/commit/?h=nfsd-testing&id=e74f668360ee592d62ed30df48b1aed86af675b5]. It carries {{Fixes:}} and {{Cc: stable}}, so it will be backported to the affected stable series (including v6.12 and v6.18) automatically once it reaches mainline.

Upstream commit message, as applied:
{code:language=none}

nfsd: don't modify a session slot when replaying its cached reply

nfsd4_sequence() claims a session slot by setting NFSD4_SLOT_INUSE
under nn->client_lock. A reply served from the slot's reply cache does
not claim it, and that distinction lived only in cstate->status, which
nfsd4_sequence() set to nfserr_replay_cache. Commit cc028a10a48c
("NFSD: Hoist status code encoding into XDR encoder functions") moved
nfsd4_proc_compound()'s cstate->status assignment below the out:
label, and the replay path's goto out was the one path that relied on
skipping it. The test in nfsd4_sequence_done() therefore no longer
identifies a replay, and every replay now stores its reply and clears
NFSD4_SLOT_INUSE as though it owned the slot.

NFSD4_SLOT_INUSE is the interlock: check_slot_seqid() rejects every
sequence id for a slot that is in use, before replay_matches_cache()
runs. A replay never sets it, so two replays can be in flight on the
same slot at once. One can read slot->sl_cred under nn->client_lock
while the other's completion frees and rebuilds it from the XDR
encoder without that lock. Two completions can also collide with each
other and release the same group_info twice. free_svc_cred() leaves
cr_uid, cr_gid and cr_flavor intact, so the reader passes every
earlier test in same_creds() and dereferences a NULL cr_group_info.
From a 6.12.91 production server:

  BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000000000000004
  CPU: 63 UID: 0 PID: 39015 Comm: nfsd
  RIP: 0010:same_creds+0x38/0xa0 [nfsd]
  RDX: 0000000000000000
  Call Trace:
   nfsd4_sequence+0x6a8/0x910 [nfsd]
   nfsd4_proc_compound+0x345/0x670 [nfsd]
   nfsd_dispatch+0x100/0x220 [nfsd]
   svc_process_common+0x311/0x700 [sunrpc]
   svc_process+0x131/0x1c0 [sunrpc]
   svc_recv+0x7ef/0x9c0 [sunrpc]
   nfsd+0xa3/0x100 [nfsd]
  Kernel panic - not syncing: Fatal exception

Since v6.14 a live session's slot table can shrink, and the unowned
store becomes a use-after-free write. nfsd4_sequence() defers the
shrink while a slot is in use, but it tests NFSD4_SLOT_INUSE, which a
replay does not set, so free_session_slots() can kfree() the slot the
replay still holds in cstate->slot.

Record the claim in cstate->slot_owned when nfsd4_sequence() accepts a
request and test that in nfsd4_sequence_done(), so only the request
that claimed the slot updates its cached reply and clears
NFSD4_SLOT_INUSE. svc_generic_init_request() zeroes the compound
response before each request, so the flag starts clear.

Fixes: [cc028a10a48c](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/cel/linux.git/commit/?id=cc028a10a48c) ("NFSD: Hoist status code encoding into XDR encoder functions")

column4: Drop the TLS client authentication EKU from TNC and default CSRs
column5:
Middleware requests both server and client authentication extended key usages in the certificate signing requests it generates, both for the TNC wildcard certificate and in the default HTTPS RSA and ECC certificate profiles, following what was then universal CA practice and a Let's Encrypt community recommendation still cited in the code. The Chrome Root Program reversed that consensus with its Moving Forward, Together initiative starting in 2022: public CAs must issue from hierarchies dedicated to server authentication, and certificates issued on or after March 15, 2027 may assert only the server authentication purpose. Every public CA has followed. ZeroSSL stopped including the client authentication EKU in October 2025, Let's Encrypt ends support in July 2026, and Google Trust Services now rejects any CSR that includes it.

TrueNAS Connect does not use mutual TLS anywhere, so nothing depends on the EKU. Remove client authentication from the TNC CSR and from the default HTTPS certificate profiles, while keeping it selectable for user generated CSRs aimed at private CAs.

The primary movtivation is to be able to use Google CA internally to get around ZeroSSL rate limits that have lead to many inconsistent test failures on internal nightlies. Let’s Encrypt’s limits are too small for more than one nightly run a week, and are shared with the domain so would affect its current role as a temporary prod fallback. Right now orders for certs against Google CA fail due to CLIENT_AUTH inclusion.

column4: Adapt UI to the middleware entitlement engine
column5:
Middleware has replaced all ad-hoc "is this Enterprise / is this licensed" checks with a single entitlement engine. {{system.product_type}} now describes hardware only, and a new endpoint reports, per feature, whether the system is entitled to it and why not. The UI should move all feature gating onto that endpoint and use product type for branding alone.

h2. Three independent signals

Middleware answers three separate questions and never mixes them. The UI should pick the right one for each decision.

* *Hardware identity* — {{system.product_type}} ({{ENTERPRISE}} / {{COMMUNITY_EDITION}}) and {{truenas.is_ix_hardware}}. Use for branding only.
* *License present* — {{truenas.license.info}} returns the license or {{null}}. Use for the license card / upload flows only.
* *Feature entitlement* — {{truenas.entitlements.info}}. Use for every show/hide or enable/disable decision about a subsystem.

h2. Methods removed or changed

* {{system.is_enterprise}} has been removed. There is no replacement; every decision it used to drive maps to one of the three signals above.
* {{system.feature_enabled}} is deprecated and private on the v26 API. Use {{truenas.entitlements.check}} or the {{info}} map.
* {{system.license_update}} now errors. License upload is {{truenas.license.upload}}.
* {{system.product_type}} keeps its two values but now reflects hardware alone: {{ENTERPRISE}} means iX appliance hardware excluding Minis, regardless of license. An unlicensed appliance reports {{ENTERPRISE}}; a licensed Mini or whitebox reports {{COMMUNITY_EDITION}}. It must not be used as a proxy for "licensed" or for "feature available".

h2. Feature gating: {{truenas.entitlements.info}}

* Role {{SYSTEM_PRODUCT_READ}}, no arguments. Returns {{{ features: { <KEY>: { entitled, reason, message } } }}}.
* {{truenas.entitlements.check(<KEY>)}} returns a single entry. An unknown key returns {{entitled: true}} with reason {{NOT_GATED}}; it never errors.
* The key set is open and grows across releases. Iterate the map, ignore keys you do not recognise, and treat an absent key as not gated. Do not model keys as a closed enum that breaks on a new value.
* {{reason}} values today: {{ENTITLED}}, {{NO_LICENSE}}, {{KEY_MISSING}}, {{WRONG_HARDWARE}}, {{TIER_INSUFFICIENT}}, {{WRONG_LICENSE_TYPE}}, {{NOT_GATED}}. More may be added; treat an unknown reason as a generic denial.
* Denial reasons should render differently:
** {{WRONG_HARDWARE}} — this hardware can never have the feature. Hide the control.
** {{KEY_MISSING}} — a license is installed but does not carry the feature. Offer a license upgrade, not a first-time purchase.
** {{NO_LICENSE}} — no license installed. Offer purchase / upload.
** {{TIER_INSUFFICIENT}} / {{WRONG_LICENSE_TYPE}} — licensed, but the contract tier or license type does not qualify. Upgrade messaging.
** {{message}} is a server-provided explanation suitable as the default tooltip.
* No event fires when entitlements change. Re-fetch {{truenas.entitlements.info}} and {{truenas.license.info}} after {{truenas.license.upload}} completes, and avoid caching the map for the whole session.

h2. Which key gates which subsystem

The UI should gate each of these surfaces on the named key and on nothing else (no product-type or hardware checks alongside it):

* {{APPS}} — Apps
* {{CONTAINERS}} — Containers
* {{VMS}} — Virtual machines
* {{DEDUP}} — Dataset deduplication
* {{KMIP}} — KMIP
* {{SED}} — Self-encrypting disk settings everywhere they appear (advanced settings, disk form, KMIP, wizard, encryption page)
* {{FIBRECHANNEL}} — Fibre Channel target mode and ports ({{fc.capable}} already includes this)
* {{ZFSTIER}} — Storage tiering
* {{RDMA}} — NFS over RDMA, iSCSI iSER, NVMe-oF RDMA transport ({{rdma.capable_protocols}} already reflects this)
* {{NVMEOF_SPDK}} — NVMe-oF SPDK backend option
* {{SMB_VEEAM}} — SMB "Veeam repository" share purpose
* {{NFS_SNAPSHOT}} — NFS "Expose Snapshots" option
* {{DIRECTORY_SERVICES}} — Directory-services login for the UI ({{system.general.ds_auth}}) and privilege DS auth
* {{NETWORK_FEC}} — Interface FEC mode
* {{WEBSHARE}} — WebShare sharing
* {{TRUESEARCH}} — Global search backend. A TrueNAS Connect connection is no longer a substitute for this entitlement.
* {{SUPPORT}} — Chooses the licensed vs community support ticket form; middleware selects the ticket path on this same key.
* {{HA}} — HA / failover. {{failover.licensed}} remains valid and reflects the same thing; do not pre-gate HA UI on product type.
* {{PROACTIVE_SUPPORT}}, {{MISSION_CRITICAL}}, {{STIG}} — already applied server-side via {{support.is_available}}, {{update.profile_choices}} ({{available}} flag) and {{system.security.info.fips_available}}. No UI change beyond not assuming Enterprise hardware implies them.
* {{CATALOG_ENTERPRISE_TRAIN}}, {{SMB_FASTPATH}} — no UI surface today; gate on the key if one is added.

h2. License payload changes

{{truenas.license.info}} is now a typed model:

* The top-level {{expires_at}} is gone. The support contract end date is {{features[SUPPORT].expires_at}}.
* Each feature entry now also carries {{source}} and {{type}} (contract tier).
* {{type}} is open-ended ({{ENTERPRISE_SINGLE}}, {{ENTERPRISE_HA}}, {{COMMERCIAL}}, {{COMMUNITY}}, {{UNKNOWN}}, more may follow). {{model}} and {{contract_type}} are nullable.
* The {{features}} list can be considerably longer than before, since legacy licenses have a fixed feature set injected server-side. Feature labels should fall back to the raw key for anything unrecognised.
* A license whose model starts with {{freenas}} is reported as no license ({{null}}). If the license daemon is unavailable the system also reports as unlicensed. Both just need the normal "no license" rendering.

The dashboard payload behind {{webui.main.dashboard.sys_info}} ({{system.license}}):

* {{expired}} is gone. Derive from {{contract_end}} if needed.
* {{contract_start}} is now a real date.
* {{contract_end}} stays and is the value the dashboard license-expiry helper should keep using.

h2. Network settings

{{network.configuration.config}} omits {{hostname_b}} and {{hostname_virtual}} entirely (keys absent, not {{null}}) unless the system is HA-capable. Read them optionally and show the fields based on {{failover.licensed}}, not product type.

h2. Branding

Product type follows hardware alone, so as shipped:

* iX appliance hardware shows Enterprise branding (logo, edition label, copyright line, hidden marketing CTAs) even with no license installed.
* A licensed Mini or whitebox shows Community Edition branding.

Anything currently hidden or shown "because Enterprise" that is really about licensing (e.g. thumbprint row, feature-vote block, upgrade CTAs) should be re-evaluated against the correct signal: hardware, license present, or a specific entitlement.

h2. References (middleware {{stable/26}})

* {{plugins/truenas/entitlements.py}} — endpoint
* {{api/v26_0_0/truenas.py}} — {{EntitlementsInfo}}, {{EntitlementEntry}}, {{LicenseInfoEntry}}, {{LicenseFeatureEntry}}
* {{utils/entitlements/engine.py}} — {{Reason}}
* {{utils/entitlements/policy.py}} — {{POLICY}}, the authoritative key list
* {{plugins/system/product.py}} — {{product_type}}, {{feature_enabled}}, {{license}}

column4: test(api): pin the secure rename shape, and who may see which complaint
column5:
27.0.0-BETA.1 PR: https://github.com/iXsystems/truenas-file-manager/pull/1660

Part of #336, acceptance 2 and 3. {{normalizeRenameShape}} goes *72.2% → 100%* and {{paramShapeError.Error()}} *0% → 100%*. Pure function, no fixtures, so these run in CI rather than skipping.

h2. What the secure rename form is for

It names a directory and a *bare* new name rather than two paths, and the function's own comment says why: _"a bare name cannot name another directory, so the rename stays where the caller said it was."_ Pinned:

* a path separator anywhere in {{newName}} is refused — parent traversal, subdirectory, absolute path, trailing slash
* a NUL byte is refused, because the kernel truncates a name there
* a relative {{path}} is *refused rather than resolved*. The deleted secure handler ran {{filepath.Abs}}, which answers against the *server's* working directory and has nothing to do with a caller's virtual path
* a request already carrying {{oldPath}} is left alone, so mixing the two shapes gets the standard reading rather than a merge
* an incomplete secure form passes through, for the handler to say precisely which field is missing
* the secure {{fileHandle}} is taken only when the caller sent none

h2. The disclosure rule, which is what {{Error()}} exists for

{{createConflictHandlerWrapper}} shows a {{*paramShapeError}} *verbatim* and replaces anything else with the generic message. So which _type_ comes back decides what a caller learns about the server. Both halves are asserted: a shape refusal must be a {{paramShapeError}}, and *a decode failure must not be* — an unmarshal error describes this package's own structs.

h2. Measured and deliberately not asserted

{{"."}} and {{".."}} survive the separator check. {{filepath.Base}} returns them unchanged, so {{filepath.Base(n) == n}} holds, and {{filepath.Join}} then collapses them. On master:

{code:language=none}
newName ".."  ->  newPath "/share"           (the parent directory)
newName "."   ->  newPath "/share/reports"   (the containing directory)
{code}

So the function's comment overstates what it guarantees. *It is not exploitable*: {{fs.CheckEntryName}} refuses {{""}}, {{"."}} and {{".."}} before the rename runs ({{file_operations_secure.go:111,114}}), and that is where the guarantee actually lives. CLAUDE.md says not to encode a hole as a test's expected result, so there is no case asserting {{".."}} is accepted — the comment above the table names the layer that carries the weight instead. Not filed as an issue either: there is no defect today, and the fix would be to tighten a comment or add two names to a check, which this note is enough to prompt.

h2. Mutation table

Each mutation was confirmed applied (the changed line printed back) before the run, and {{git status --porcelain}} was empty after every restore.

||#||Mutation||Killed||
|M1|the separator check removed|the four traversal subtests — *and* the disclosure case, correctly: it uses {{../b.txt}} to _produce_ a shape error, so removing the check removes its input|
|M2|the absolute-path check removed|the relative-path case alone|
|M3|{{oldPath}} no longer short-circuits|the standard-rename case alone|
|M4|the NUL check looks for a rune that never appears|the NUL case alone — *see below*|
|M5|the secure handle overwrites the caller's|the fileHandle case alone|
|M6|a decode failure dressed as a {{paramShapeError}}|the disclosure case — this is the half that proves the _second_ assertion carries weight|

*M4 read as a survivor first, and that was my measurement being wrong, not the code.* Deleting the check made {{strings}} an unused import, so the package stopped compiling; my runner counts {{--- FAIL}} lines, and a build failure produces none. Recut to keep the import used — the same call looking for {{'￿'}} — with {{go build}} as an explicit control before the run, it kills the NUL case and nothing else. This is the third time a non-compiling mutation has scored as whatever I happened to be counting; the control is now part of the cut rather than an afterthought.

h2. Verification

* {{go build ./...}}, {{go vet ./...}}, {{go test ./... -count=1}} — every package in {{truenas-file-manager}} green
* {{golangci-lint run --config ../.golangci.yml ./...}} — *0 issues under 2.9.0, the version CI pins*
* 26/26 repo self-tests
* 15 cases counted rather than assumed — 8 top-level, 7 subtests
* Composes onto master

column4: Web UI unavailable after OS upgrade on systems with many RSA-4096 certificates
column5:
Product / version

TrueNAS SCALE 26.0.0-BETA.3

I have observed the same user-visible failure after upgrades to BETA.1, BETA.2, and BETA.3.

Summary

After upgrading TrueNAS, the Web UI becomes unavailable because nginx cannot start:

open() "/etc/nginx/nginx.conf" failed (2: No such file or directory)

/etc/nginx/nginx.conf is generated by middleware rather than being present in the pristine /etc dataset.

On this system, generating the nginx configuration takes approximately 67 seconds because certificate lookup is unexpectedly expensive. The configured UI certificate is looked up twice during nginx rendering, and each filtered lookup takes approximately 34 seconds.

The main performance issue is reproducible independently of nginx:

certificate.query([["id","=",50]])                    ~33.9 s
certificate.query([])                                 ~34.1 s
certificate.query([["id","=",50]],
                  {"force_sql_filters":true})           2.9 s

The filtered query therefore costs essentially the same as querying every certificate unless force_sql_filters is explicitly enabled.

This appears to cause the automatic nginx-generation path during creation of a new boot environment to fail or time out. No nginx.conf is produced, so the management UI is unavailable.

Manually running nginx generation with a sufficiently long API timeout succeeds without changing any certificate or UI configuration, and the Web UI immediately works again.

Environment

Affected system:

TrueNAS-26.0.0-BETA.3

Certificate inventory:

17 certificate/CSR records total
16 RSA-4096
1 RSA-2048

All certificate and CSR records parse successfully. I found no corrupt certificate.

The affected system is relatively low-powered hardware, which makes the performance problem particularly visible, but the query behavior itself does not appear hardware-specific.

A second TrueNAS system with a different certificate inventory does not exhibit the failure.

User-visible failure

Immediately after an OS upgrade:

{noformat}ls -l /etc/nginx/nginx.conf{noformat}

returns:

{noformat}No such file or directory{noformat}

and:

{noformat}systemctl status nginx{noformat}

shows nginx failed because it cannot open:

{noformat}/etc/nginx/nginx.conf{noformat}

SMB and other services continue to operate. The failure is specifically the management Web UI/nginx path.

This has recurred after multiple TrueNAS 26 beta upgrades.

nginx configuration is generated, not shipped in pristine /etc

On BETA.3, nginx configuration is generated from middleware:

{noformat}/usr/lib/python3/dist-packages/middlewared/etc_files/local/nginx/nginx.conf.mako{noformat}

and is registered for the INTERFACE_SYNC checkpoint.

The expected output is:

{noformat}/etc/nginx/nginx.conf{noformat}

The nginx file is also absent from the pristine /etc boot-environment state, so a newly-created boot environment depends on successful first-time generation.

Certificate query performance

Raw certificate datastore access is fast.

The expensive operation occurs during certificate extension/normalization.

Timing the normal public API query:

{noformat}time midclt call certificate.query '[["id","=",20]]' >/dev/null{noformat}

result:

{noformat}~33.921 s{noformat}

Querying all certificates:

{noformat}time midclt call certificate.query '[]' >/dev/null{noformat}

result:

{noformat}~34.067 s{noformat}

A query for one certificate therefore takes essentially exactly the same time as querying the entire 17-record certificate inventory.

I then tested the same primary-key query using SQL filter pushdown:

{noformat}time midclt call certificate.query \\
  '[["id","=",50]]' \\
  '{"force_sql_filters":true}' >/dev/null{noformat}

result:

{noformat}2.902 s total{noformat}

This is approximately an 11.7x improvement and strongly indicates that, without force_sql_filters, unrelated certificate records are being extended before the filter is applied.

No certificate configuration was changed for this test.

Source of the per-certificate cost

certificate.cert_extend() calls certificate normalization, which loads private keys.

I benchmarked each certificate/CSR independently.

Typical results:

RSA-4096 certificate/CSR: ~2.04-2.06 s
RSA-2048 certificate:     ~0.28 s

All parsed successfully.

I isolated the expensive cryptography operation further using the same RSA-4096 private key:

load_pem_private_key(..., unsafe_skip_rsa_key_validation=False)
    ~2.0464 s

load_pem_private_key(..., unsafe_skip_rsa_key_validation=True)
    ~0.0003 s

I am NOT proposing unsafe_skip_rsa_key_validation=True as the fix. This test only demonstrates that almost all of the per-record cost comes from full RSA private-key validation during ordinary certificate query extension.

With 16 RSA-4096 records, this explains the ~34-second full-extension time.

Why nginx generation takes ~67 seconds

The nginx template retrieves the configured UI certificate.

The subsequent service-certificate validation path retrieves the same certificate again.

On this system, each lookup without SQL filter pushdown costs approximately 34 seconds.

Therefore the measured nginx-generation time is approximately:

~34 s first certificate lookup

* ~34 s validation lookup

----

~68 s

The actual measured full nginx generation was:

{noformat}1:07.07{noformat}

which closely matches that prediction.

Manual reproduction / recovery

Without changing the UI certificate or any certificate data, I ran:

{code:python}from truenas_api_client import Client

with Client(private_methods=True, call_timeout=180) as c:
    print(c.call("etc.generate", "nginx")){code}

Result:

{noformat}[{'path': '/etc/nginx/nginx.conf',
  'status': 'CHANGED',
  'changes': ['CONTENTS']}]{noformat}

Elapsed time:

{noformat}~67.07 s{noformat}

Then:

{noformat}nginx -t
systemctl restart nginx{noformat}

nginx -t succeeded and the normal HTTPS Web UI immediately became available.

No certificate was replaced.
No UI HTTPS setting was changed.
No database modification was required.

Reboot behavior

After generating /etc/nginx/nginx.conf, I recorded its checksum:

{noformat}2efb1cace50e2af26ad4e78aa13f7972153fb93e33021e5373182a026f835dd5{noformat}

I then rebooted normally.

The Web UI came back successfully.

This indicates that once nginx.conf exists in the current boot environment, ordinary reboot is not the problem.

The failure occurs when an OS upgrade creates a new boot environment whose /etc does not yet contain the generated nginx configuration.

Recurrence across upgrades

This same symptom has occurred after upgrades to:

26.0.0-BETA.1
26.0.0-BETA.2
26.0.0-BETA.3

Previously, resetting to defaults and then restoring the saved TrueNAS configuration also recovered the UI.

A plausible explanation is that the default configuration has a much smaller certificate inventory, allowing nginx configuration generation to complete before the full saved configuration is restored.

The BETA.3 reproduction above does not depend on that hypothesis: direct generation with an extended timeout conclusively restores the UI.

Root causes

# Primary-key certificate queries do not push the filter down before expensive extension

This is the most directly demonstrated problem.

Measured:

certificate.query(id=50), normal:
    ~33.9 s

certificate.query(id=50), force_sql_filters=true:
    2.902 s

A query for one certificate should not require extension and RSA validation of every unrelated certificate in the datastore.

# Ordinary certificate.query performs expensive private-key validation

Certificate normalization loads private keys even for ordinary read/query operations.

On this system, each RSA-4096 private key costs approximately 2.05 seconds to validate.

This makes certificate-list/query latency scale approximately linearly with the number of RSA-4096 private keys.

Full cryptographic private-key validation appears unnecessarily expensive for a read-only operation whose immediate purpose includes obtaining metadata such as key type and key size.

# nginx processes the selected certificate twice

nginx obtains the configured UI certificate and the service-validation path subsequently performs another lookup for the same certificate.

With the current query behavior, this approximately doubles rendering time from ~34 seconds to ~67 seconds.

# Failure of nginx generation can leave the appliance with no management UI

Because a new boot environment initially has no generated /etc/nginx/nginx.conf, failure or timeout during initial rendering leaves nginx unable to start at all.

Certificate processing performance should not be able to make the appliance's management interface completely unavailable.

Proposed minimal patch

The lowest-risk immediate fix is to push primary-key certificate filters into SQL before certificate extension.

This retains the existing private-key validation behavior for the selected certificate and does not bypass any cryptographic checks.

For the nginx UI-certificate lookup:

{noformat}- cert = middleware.call_sync(
-     'certificate.query',
-     [['id', '=', general_settings['ui_certificate']]],
- )
+ cert = middleware.call_sync(
+     'certificate.query',
+     [['id', '=', general_settings['ui_certificate']]],
+     {'force_sql_filters': True},
+ ){noformat}

Likewise, in certificate.cert_services_validation():

{noformat}- cert = await self.middleware.call(
-     'certificate.query',
-     [['id', '=', id_]],
- )
+ cert = await self.middleware.call(
+     'certificate.query',
+     [['id', '=', id_]],
+     {'force_sql_filters': True},
+ ){noformat}

This patch is supported by an actual before/after measurement on the affected system:

normal filtered certificate query:
    ~33.9 s

same query with force_sql_filters:
    2.902 s

Expected nginx certificate-processing cost on this system would therefore fall approximately from:

{noformat}~34 + ~34 = ~68 s{noformat}

to:

{noformat}~2.9 + ~2.9 = ~5.8 s{noformat}

without weakening certificate validation.

Recommended additional improvements

# Avoid the duplicate certificate lookup

The nginx renderer already has the expanded certificate object.

certificate.cert_services_validation() should ideally accept that object rather than querying the same certificate again.

Conceptually:

{noformat}async def cert_services_validation(
    self, id_, schema_name, raise_verrors=True, cert=None
):
    if cert is None:
        certs = await self.middleware.call(
            'certificate.query',
            [['id', '=', id_]],
            {'force_sql_filters': True},
        )
        cert = certs[0] if certs else None{noformat}

The nginx renderer could then pass the certificate it already retrieved.

That should reduce this path to one certificate expansion rather than two.

# Avoid full private-key validation during ordinary query/list operations

A broader architectural improvement would be to avoid fully validating every private key whenever certificates are listed.

For properties such as:

{noformat}key_type
key_length{noformat}

the information can generally be obtained from the certificate or CSR public key.

Full private-key validation and certificate/private-key matching would be more appropriate at:

{code:python}create
import
update
explicit certificate validation
service configuration changes{code}

rather than every ordinary certificate.query.

Caching or persisting derived key metadata would also avoid repeatedly performing the same expensive work.

I would not recommend merely switching ordinary queries to unsafe_skip_rsa_key_validation=True; avoiding unnecessary private-key loading entirely appears safer and cleaner.

# Add boot-time resilience

Even with the performance fixes, failure to process a configured TLS certificate should not leave TrueNAS without any Web UI.

Possible safeguards include:

* giving the interface-sync etc-generation call an explicit sufficiently long timeout;
* retaining the previous valid generated nginx configuration until a replacement is successfully rendered;
* generating a temporary HTTP-only management configuration if TLS configuration generation fails;
* raising an alert explaining the certificate problem rather than leaving nginx unable to start.

Increasing a timeout alone would mitigate this particular outage but would not fix the underlying certificate-query scalability problem.

Expected behavior

A query such as:

{noformat}certificate.query([["id","=",50]]){noformat}

should extend only certificate ID 50.

Rendering nginx configuration should not repeatedly parse every unrelated private key.

If certificate rendering nevertheless fails, TrueNAS should retain a usable management interface rather than leaving /etc/nginx/nginx.conf absent.

Actual behavior

A primary-key-filtered certificate query extends enough records that it takes essentially as long as querying the complete certificate table:

ID-filtered: ~33.9 s
all records: ~34.1 s

Enabling SQL filter pushdown reduces the same filtered query to:

2.902 s

nginx consequently takes approximately 67 seconds to generate.

After an OS update/new boot environment, automatic generation does not successfully produce /etc/nginx/nginx.conf, nginx fails to start, and the Web UI is unavailable.

Current workaround

From SSH or local console:

{code:python}from truenas_api_client import Client

with Client(private_methods=True, call_timeout=180) as c:
    print(c.call("etc.generate", "nginx")){code}

followed by:

{noformat}nginx -t
systemctl restart nginx{noformat}

This restores the normal configured HTTPS Web UI and survives subsequent ordinary reboots.

The workaround currently has to be repeated after a new OS upgrade/boot environment.

column4: Editing a user changes the user's home directory to the parent
column5:
Edit User form submits the parent of the home directory path, so saving an unrelated change relocates the user's home and re-permissions the parent directory



This is on a system migrated from TrueNAS Core. Reproduced in both Firefox and Safari, latest versions, on macOS. Not browser-specific.

h2. Steps to reproduce

# Credentials > Users > Add. Username {{test_home_user}}. Tick *Create Home Directory*, leave the path at the pre-filled {{/mnt/tank/home}}, Default Permissions 700. Save.
# Confirm the account was created correctly. {{user.query}} returns {{home = /mnt/tank/home/test_home_user}} and that directory exists, owned by the new user. This step works as documented.
# Credentials > Users > {{test_home_user}} > Edit. Observe the Home Directory field reads {{/mnt/tank/home}}, not {{/mnt/tank/home/test_home_user}}.
# Change one unrelated setting only. I ticked Shell Access. Do not touch the home directory field.
# Click Save.

h2. Expected

Step 3: the field shows the stored value, {{/mnt/tank/home/test_home_user}}.

Step 5: only the Shell Access change is applied. No warning, no home directory change.

h2. Actual

Step 3: the field shows {{/mnt/tank/home}}, the parent.

Step 5:

{noformat}Warning!
Operation will change permissions on path: '/mnt/tank/home'{noformat}

Screenshot attached, showing the Edit panel and the warning together.

{{getHomeCreateWarning()}} in {{src/app/pages/credentials/users/user-form/user-form.component.ts}} returns that string from exactly one branch:

typescript

{noformat}if (!homeCreate && editingUser.home !== home) {
  return this.translate.instant(
    'Operation will change permissions on path: {path}',
    { path: `'${String(home)}'` },
  );
}{noformat}

For it to fire and name {{/mnt/tank/home}}, three things must hold: {{home_create}} is false, {{editingUser.home}} is {{/mnt/tank/home/test_home_user}}, and the value the form is about to submit is {{/mnt/tank/home}}.

The form is submitting the parent. The home path field round-trips incorrectly: it is populated with the parent but {{user.update}} treats the submitted value as the literal home when {{home_create}} is false.

h2. Impact

Any save on any user relocates that user's home to the parent directory. {{user.update}} then calls {{user.do_home_copy}}, which runs {{copytree}} from the old home to the new one, so the user's entire home directory is copied into a location shared with every other user. {{setup_homedir}} also calls {{filesystem.setperm}} with {{stripacl: True}} against the new path, which on a shared parent locks every other user out of their own home.

This is a test account, but I just had to clean up from this happening on a real user account when I changed the account to “Full Admin”. It moved the user’s home directory to /mnt/tank/home and copied the contents and changed permissions on the home directory itself.
